title: A Note for His Mother
hook: a mother begs her son to come home; he answers on a scrap of paper
carry: karma or effort? first ask who the doer is
tomorrow: at sixteen, a healthy boy lies down as if dead. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a scholar who'd read everything, and jnana: know the knower, not just the facts. Today, a mother comes to the hill.

1898, the hill at Tiruvannamalai. A woman finds the son who vanished from home two years before. He was sixteen when he left a note and took the train. Now he's a thin young ascetic who hardly speaks. His mother, Alagammal, weeps and begs: come home. Day after day she asks. He says nothing. At last someone hands him a pencil and paper, and he writes her an answer.
screen: `1898: A MOTHER FINDS HER SON.` → `COME HOME. DAY AFTER DAY.` → `A PENCIL, A SCRAP OF PAPER.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the note says: the Ordainer guides each soul by its karma. What's destined not to happen won't, however hard you try; what's destined to happen will, however you try to stop it. So the best course is to stay silent. She went home. And there's Hinduism's old quarrel on one scrap of paper. One side stresses karma already in motion, called prarabdha: seeds planted long ago, bearing fruit now. At its best, that view brings humility, and stops people blaming themselves for what they couldn't control. The other side stresses effort: nothing grows without work, and the next step is still taken today. Decades later Ramana gave the quarrel one verse in his Forty Verses. In paraphrase: the argument over which wins, fate or free will, belongs only to those who don't know the root of both. Know the self, the root of fate and effort alike, and you're free of both. Look at the move. Both sides assume a doer in the middle, a karta, pushed by fate or pushing back. Ramana asks who that doer is. Near the poem's end he says: if we're the doers, we taste the fruit; when, by asking who the doer is, the self is known, the sense of being the doer drops, and all three kinds of karma with it. Many readers hear the note to his mother the same way: not a shrug, but a son who no longer took himself to be the one steering. And the story didn't end there. Years later Alagammal came to live near him on the hill, and stayed for the rest of her life.
screen: `THE NOTE: WHAT'S MEANT TO BE, WILL BE.` · `PRARABDHA: KARMA IN MOTION.` · `EFFORT: THE STEP TAKEN NOW.` · `BOTH ASSUME A DOER.` · then, large: `ASK WHO THE DOER IS.`

segments.voice: Do one small thing within reach: straighten a cup, close a drawer, fold the corner of a blanket. Do it slowly. For the rest of the sit, watch for the thought that says I did that, and ask, gently, who.
Ramana's Forty Verses: a poem that meets the fate-or-effort quarrel by asking who the doer is.
Pocket this: karma or effort? First ask who the doer is, the way Ramana's verse does. Rest well tonight.
